title: How a dynamic workflow runs, and what the transporter room shows of it

beats.label: The script
beats.title: A script is in charge
beats.text: The lead writes a JavaScript script. Its meta names it and declares its phases (with a detail each) before anything runs. Claude Code saves the script and runs it in the background.
beats.narration: On the left is the script the lead hands to Claude Code. The top part, the meta, names the workflow and lists its phases up front, each with a short description. Claude Code saves the script, then runs it in the background while the lead carries on.

beats.label: agent() calls
beats.title: Each agent() call queues an agent
beats.text: phase() sets the label; each agent() call queues a Claude agent with a label, phase and output schema. At most 16 run at once (4 here so you can see the queue); the rest wait.
beats.narration: Each time the script calls agent, a new Claude agent is queued, with a label, the phase it belongs to and the shape of answer it must return. Only so many run at once, sixteen normally, four here so you can watch a queue form. In the middle, the queue on top is the room's pattern buffer, and the slots below are the pads.

beats.label: Data flows back
beats.title: Results flow back into the script
beats.text: Each agent returns a JSON value to the script, which decides what to do next. In a pipeline, a review's result immediately starts its verifier, so phases overlap.
beats.narration: When an agent finishes, its answer goes back into the script as data. That's the part that makes it dynamic: the script reads the result and decides what to run next. In this pipeline each finished review starts its own verifier straight away, so the review and verify phases overlap.

beats.label: Log + journal
beats.title: The script narrates, the journal remembers
beats.text: log() lines are the script's own commentary. Claude Code journals every start and result, so a re-run can resume and reuse cached results.
beats.narration: Down the bottom left, the script can log its own commentary, like how many reviews came back. Claude Code also keeps a journal of every agent's start and result, which is what lets a workflow resume later without redoing the finished work.

beats.label: Return
beats.title: Its return value goes to the lead
beats.text: The script returns a value. Claude Code gives the lead a new turn with that result, plus totals: tokens, tool calls and time.
beats.narration: Finally the script returns a value. Claude Code wakes the lead with that result in a new turn, along with totals for tokens, tool calls and time taken.

beats.label: Gaps
beats.title: What the room shows, and what it doesn't
beats.text: Shown today: the queue (pattern buffer), agents at work (pads), phase counts (tactical display). Not shown: the script itself, data flowing back, logs, journal and the returned result.
beats.narration: So here's where the transporter room stands. The queue, the agents at work and the counts per phase are all there: the pattern buffer, the pads and the tactical display. What's missing is the controller: the script itself, the results flowing back into it, its log lines, and what it finally hands back to the lead.
